components.text: The earlier move's decisive demand is whether historical abstraction supports treating the God concept as a human construction.
The earlier move's decisive demand is whether repeated cultural emergence and evolution support human invention of religions.
Whether an increasingly abstract God concept supports the conclusion that God is a changing human construction.
Whether repeated cultural evolution of religions supports their classification as human inventions.
The decisive inference is that a beginning of this universe's space and time supplies scientific support for divine creation.
Whether a beginning of matter, space, and time supplies scientific support for a divine creator.
The decisive demand is whether observed life-permitting conditions require or comparatively favor an intelligent creator.
Whether life-permitting cosmic conditions are more simply explained by deliberate creator design.
The decisive demand is whether Darwinian material explanations can account for free will, choice, consciousness, and intentionality.
Whether consciousness, free will, choice, and intentionality lack adequate Darwinian or material explanation.
The legal earlier target demands an account of consciousness, intentional choice, and responsibility under material processes.
Whether moral responsibility and intentional choice can be reduced to deterministic material processes.
The earlier move's decisive demand is whether human representatives and shared reasoning make divine moral instruction unnecessary.
The earlier move disputes a bare dismissal of Darwinian explanations for consciousness and intentionality.
Whether human rational deliberation and unavoidable human mediation make divine moral instruction unnecessary.
Whether widespread cultural production of religions supports their human-invention status.
The decisive inference is that proliferation and variation among religions support treating religions as human inventions.
The decisive inference is that historical variation in God concepts supports their status as human constructions.
Whether the multiplicity and recurrent development of religions support rejecting them as human inventions.
Whether historical transformation of the God concept supports its status as an evolving construction.
The earlier move's decisive demand concerns whether shared human reasoning can evaluate morality without divine instruction.
The earlier move's decisive demand concerns whether substantive Darwinian explanations exist for mental phenomena.
Whether shared public reasoning provides a sufficient secular basis for moral judgment without divine instruction.
Whether existing naturalistic research answers claims that consciousness and intentionality resist material explanation.
The decisive inference is that subjective access makes consciousness irreducible and renders scientific demands for public support selectively inappropriate.
The decisive demand is whether consciousness is inaccessible to material or scientific explanation.
The decisive demand is whether inward experience must receive serious evidential consideration.
Whether consciousness is an irreducible subjective starting point that makes skepticism about God selectively demanding.
Whether consciousness cannot be adequately explained through material or Darwinian processes.
The decisive inference is that a humanly evolving concept of God supports treating its alleged object as a human construction.
The decisive inference is that natural evolution of religious forms establishes that the whole religious object is undesigned or unreal.
The decisive demand is whether Darwinian explanation of parts removes the need for an explanation of the universe as a whole.
Whether the human cultural origin and evolution of religions establishes that their purported divine object is invented.
Whether historical abstraction of the God concept establishes that its referent is a human construction.
Whether natural processes within possible universes remove the need to explain the universe as a designed whole.
The decisive demand is whether human rational deliberation can provide an adequate secular account of morality.
The decisive demand is whether Darwinian explanation can account for responsibility and morally significant agency.
The decisive demand is whether scientific explanation exhausts the allegedly irreducible mental phenomena.
Whether human rational deliberation can adequately ground morality without continuing supernatural authority.
Whether Darwinian explanation adequately accounts for morality and responsible agency.
The decisive demand is whether evolutionary accounts can explain morality beyond simple reciprocity and gene-serving behavior.
The decisive demand is whether material processes can adequately explain intentional and responsible agency.
Whether evolutionary accounts can explain morality beyond reciprocal or kin-centered low altruism.
Whether morality and responsibility resist Darwinian or material explanation.
The decisive demand is whether secular rational deliberation can sustain morality without divine instruction or authority.
The decisive demand is whether evolutionary genesis plus political endorsement adequately explains and sustains morality.
Whether secular rational deliberation can sustain morality without divine instruction or authority.
Whether explaining moral genesis and deliberating politically suffice to preserve equality, dignity, and compassion.
The decisive demand is whether public evidential standards selectively exclude beliefs grounded in subjective consciousness.
The decisive demand is whether religious experience deserves evidential consideration rather than dismissal.
The decisive demand is whether secular culture can safely sustain inherited moral commitments without religious belief.
Whether secular culture can retain equality, dignity, and compassion after abandoning belief in God.
Whether religious experience deserves serious evidential consideration despite external skeptical analogies.
The decisive demand is whether scientific study of conscious machinery supports a reducible, materially explained account of consciousness.
The decisive demand is whether naturalistic work can explain consciousness, choice, and intentionality.
The decisive demand is whether self-correcting inquiry has an epistemic advantage over protected faith commitments.
Whether studying the machinery of consciousness supports a one-way material explanation without irreducible mental causation.
Whether naturalistic explanatory progress adequately accounts for consciousness and intentional causation.
